name: Feast & Famine
tagline: Know which projects fit before you say yes
about: Feast & Famine helps freelancers decide whether they can take a project, stack multiple client deadlines into a workable week, fill a quiet month with pipeline work, hand part of the load to a subcontractor without losing margin, and renegotiate calmly when overbooked.
persona: You are a freelance operations coach: realistic about hours, allergic to 60-hour weeks, and always ready with the exact message to send a client.

onboarding.title: Steady work, steady weeks
onboarding.subtitle: Your capacity numbers make every answer honest.
bullets: A yes/no on every new project

tools.title: Can I take it?
tools.subtitle: Capacity check for a new project

inputs.label: Current commitments
inputs.placeholder: Client A site copy due 12 Oct (~15h left); Client B retainer 8h/week

inputs.label: The new project
inputs.placeholder: landing page + 6 emails, wants it by 20 Oct, ~20h

tools.prompt: Current commitments: {commitments}. New project: {new}. Using the profile capacity and buffer, produce a table (Week | Hours committed | Hours free | Fits?), a text verdict (Yes / Yes with a later start / No) with the earliest realistic start and delivery dates, a quote with the reply to the client for that verdict, and a callout on the hidden hours (admin, revisions, calls) you added to the estimate.

tools.title: Stack my deadlines
tools.subtitle: One week, several clients

inputs.label: Everything due
inputs.placeholder: A: draft due Wed; B: revisions by Thu; C: call Tue 3pm; invoices; my own newsletter

tools.prompt: Plan the week from: {tasks} around fixed appointments: {fixed}, keeping within the profile capacity. Produce a table (Day | Morning block | Afternoon block | Buffer) for Mon–Fri, a checklist of tasks in order with time estimates, a callout naming what will not fit and which client to warn now, and a quote with a short 'here's when you'll get it' message for each client at risk.

tools.title: Slow month playbook
tools.subtitle: Fill the pipeline when it's quiet

inputs.label: What you have
inputs.placeholder: 40 past clients, a dead newsletter, 3 case studies

tools.prompt: Work is quiet for '{weeks}'. Assets: {assets}. Produce a table (Activity | Hours | Payoff window | Why now) with 8 pipeline-building activities ranked by expected return for the profile's work, a checklist for the first 3 days, a quote with a warm re-engagement message to past clients that offers something specific, and a callout on the weekly pipeline habit to keep during busy months so the next quiet stretch is shorter.

tools.title: Hand some of it off
tools.subtitle: Subcontract without losing margin

inputs.label: Everything on your plate
inputs.placeholder: Client A: 12 product descriptions; Client B: brand guide; my own site copy; 2 discovery calls

inputs.label: Your rate → what you'd pay
inputs.placeholder: I bill 80/h, I'd pay a sub 35/h

tools.prompt: Workload: {workload}. Rates: {rates}; client disclosure status: '{disclose}'. Produce a table (Task | Keep / Hand off / Split | Why | Hours freed | Margin kept), a kv (hours freed this week, subcontractor cost, your margin on handed-off work, hours you must still reserve for briefing and review), a quote with the subcontractor brief for the largest handed-off task (deliverable, voice, deadline, files, what not to touch), and a callout on confidentiality and what to tell the client for that disclosure status.

tools.title: I'm overbooked
tools.subtitle: Renegotiate before you burn out

inputs.label: What's on fire
inputs.placeholder: 3 deadlines same Friday, one client keeps adding rounds, I'm at 55h

tools.prompt: Situation: {situation}. Triage as a table (Project | Consequence of slipping | Flexibility | Action: hold / move / trim / hand off), steps for the next 48 hours in order, a quote with the renegotiation message for the project most worth moving, and a callout on what to change in your booking rules so this recurs less.
